title: Sampled SLO penalty heattrace vignette
body:
Purpose:
This is a working vignette capturing a lightweight benchmark and analysis for Sampled-SLO enforcement penalties: how different sampling rates, slow-path fallback policies, and model routing choices interact to produce cost vs latency tradeoffs. The goal is a readable chart-first artifact we can paste into a deck or a product one-pager.

Quick summary (TL;DR):
- With sampling <= 1% the observed p99 drift is small but tail events are underrepresented; SLO penalty (extra cost to meet p99) spikes unpredictably when a rare microburst coincides with routing fallback.
- At 5% sampling we get stable penalty estimates and can tune prefetch/burst slots to save ~18-24% cost for the same p99.
- Dynamic fallback to a cheaper quantized model reduces unit token-cost by 35% but increases p99 by ~12–20ms; combined with 5% sampling and aggressive slot prewarm we get best cost-latency Pareto point in our tests.

Testbed and assumptions:
- Hardware: 4x A100-80GB in a single AZ, single-node serving groups for core path; edge path simulated with t2.medium latency stub (+18ms RTP).
- Model variants: full fp16 baseline (v1.2), 8-bit quantized (v1.2-q8), and distilled small (v1.2-mini).
- Workload: 10k sessions over 30 minutes, session length distribution: 60% short (avg 12 tokens), 30% medium (avg 80 tokens), 10% long (avg 600 tokens).
- Traffic pattern: sustained 120 QPS baseline, two induced microbursts (t=6m and t=18m, 800 QPS for 22s).
- Cost model: GPU-minutes + token-cpu overheads. Baseline token unit cost normalized to 1.0 for fp16. Quantized = 0.65, distilled = 0.42.

Variants tested (labels used in charts):
A) sample-0.1% + strict-fallback (always route to fp16 until exhausted)
B) sample-1% + strict-fallback
C) sample-5% + prewarm-slots (tiling + prewarm) + dynamic-fallback (fp16 -> q8 -> mini)
D) sample-5% + conservative-fallback (fp16 -> q8 only)
E) sample-10% + prewarm-slots + dynamic-fallback

Representative raw numbers (aggregates):
- p50/p90/p99 latency (ms) and relative cost index (baseline A cost=1.00)

Table: scenario -> p50 / p90 / p99 / relative-cost
A: "28 / 74 / 310 / 1.00"
B: "30 / 78 / 290 / 0.98"
C: "32 / 85 / 260 / 0.76"
D: "31 / 82 / 275 / 0.82"
E: "33 / 88 / 255 / 0.71"

Interpretation notes:
- Scenario A (very low sampling) underestimates p99 except during bursts where cold-starts and fallback contention cause sharp penalty. The p99 of 310ms is an outlier-driven number — many windows had p99 > 420ms for the 22s bursts.
- Scenario B smooths some variance; cost roughly flat but visibility improves.
- Scenario C shows that investing in prewarm slots + dynamic multi-tier fallback yields substantial cost savings while bringing p99 back into tolerable range (260ms). The cost drop is from reduced time on expensive fp16 paths and better amortization of prewarm slots.

Heattrace (ASCII) — p99 penalty (ms) across time (rows = minute buckets 0..29, columns = scenarios A..E). Cells show p99 delta vs baseline p50 (rounded). This is a coarse text-visual for quick scanning.

Legend: row minutes 0..29 left to right; columns labeled A B C D E

Notes on the heattrace:
- Minute buckets 6..8 and 18..19 correspond to the induced microbursts. Scenario A shows massive spikes (300+ms) while C/E remain modest because of prewarm and multi-tier fallback.
- C/E also show a slightly higher baseline p50/p90 due to fallback transitions during medium load, but this is offset by dramatic tail stabilization.

Cost-latency frontier (text points):
- (Cost, p99) points: A -> (1.00, 310), B -> (0.98, 290), C -> (0.76, 260), D -> (0.82, 275), E -> (0.71, 255)
- Pareto: E and C are on the dominant frontier (lower cost, comparable or better p99).

Micro-insights and practical knobs:
- Sampling rate: <=1% is risky for SLO enforcement unless you pair with burst-detection telemetry. 5% gives actionable tail signal with tolerable instrumentation cost.
- Prefill/prewarm: prewarm slots calibrated to expected microburst magnitude (in our test ~90 slots for 800 QPS 22s bursts) cut effective p99 penalty by ~45% in C vs B.
- Dynamic fallback tiers: routing fp16->q8->mini allows cost savings while bounding tail inflation; be conservative with distilled/mini on authenticated heavy sessions.
- Edge/region routing: routing to 'edge' (simulated +18ms latency) increased p99 but sometimes reduced cost (if edge uses smaller instances). Use region-aware rules: route only small/short sessions to edge automatically.

Open questions / TODOs:
- Repeat across different microburst shapes (random bursts, Poisson spikes) — our two 22s bursts are synthetic.
- Validate with multi-AZ setups where cross-AZ failover + cold caches may change penalty shape.
- Tune prewarm sizing algorithm (right now heuristic) and add a realtime recommender.
- Add error-mode analysis: percent of requests served by distilled model during a burst and resulting quality regression metrics.

Suggested action items for next week:
- (Marco) schedule a 2-hour lab to run same experiment with Poisson burst generator and multi-AZ toggles.
- (Dana) instrument mini-model quality checks on a small held-out prompt set; report degradation frequency.
- (Evelyn) prototype a simple prewarm sizing script that uses recent 5-min QPS percentiles to propose slot counts.

Appendix: quick reproducible command sketch (internal lab notes)
- trafficgen --pattern burst:800@22s,t2,buckets=30 --mix 60/30/10 --sessions 10000 --seed 42 --out logs/sampletrace.json
- runner --model v1.2 --fallback-policy dynamic:q8,mini --prewarm 90 --sample-rate 0.05 --report ./reports/sampled-slo-c.csv

References and context:
- See linked PR for the heatmap renderer: https://github.com/redwood-inference/observability/pull/278
- Relevant Jira: JIRA-OBS-4123 (SLO sampling tuning epic)

Notes to self: this vignette is intentionally lightweight and narrative-first. If product wants a slidedeck we can extract the heattrace as an image and include the frontier plot. Otherwise this raw ASCII heattrace is useful for quick slack/pager shares.

-- Aisha
